In the Supreme Court of the United States

NO. 25-417
FRANCIS NIELSEN, PETITIONER
v.
KEKAI WATANABE

ON WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE NINTH CIRCUIT

BRIEF FOR THE RESPONDENT

INTRODUCTION
For Bivens, this Court has been clear: This far and no
further. The Court has consistently refused to extend
Bivens to any new context. But it also has repeatedly
declined calls to overturn the doctrine entirely, choosing
instead to preserve it in the three discrete contexts in
which it originally arose. Relevant here, since Carlson v.
Green was decided in 1980, federal prisoners in federally
operated prisons have been able to pursue damages
claims against individual federal officers for deliberate
indifference to a serious medical need in violation of the
Eighth Amendment.
Respondent Kekai Watanabe’s case arises in this prototypical Carlson context. While incarcerated in federal
prison, Watanabe suffered a serious injury: a broken

2

bone that caused months of excruciating pain. Petitioner Francis Nielsen was deliberately indifferent to
Watanabe’s injury, in violation of his Eighth Amendment rights. Watanabe asserts the same kind of violation of the same constitutional right by the same type of
defendant in the same institutional setting pursuant to
the same substantive standards as the plaintiff in Carlson. This is precisely the kind of claim this Court has
long understood Carlson to encompass.
It is also the kind of claim Congress has twice acted
to preserve and define. In 1988, Congress passed the
Westfall Act to eliminate the traditional state commonlaw remedies that prisoners historically could have pursued against federal officers. But the Act expressly preserved federal constitutional claims like those in Carlson. And in 1996, Congress passed the Prison Litigation
Reform Act (PLRA), responding in part to this Court’s
decision in McCarthy v. Madigan rejecting an exhaustion requirement for Carlson claims. Under the PLRA,
prisoners must exhaust administrative remedies before
pursuing a Carlson claim and may not recover emotional or mental damages unless they suffer a physical
injury. Congress has therefore weighed the competing
policy interests surrounding Carlson and determined
that the claims should survive, subject to procedural
and substantive limitations.
Nielsen and the United States incorrectly assert that
Watanabe’s claim arises in a new context. But each of
their proposed distinctions either is not a difference at
all, is not meaningfully different from the factors analyzed in Carlson, or would require contravening Congress’s own policy judgments made in reliance on Carlson. By their own admission, their position would not

3

just limit Carlson to its context but instead render Carlson claims a “null set.” U.S. Br. 25. Such a result would
conflict with this Court’s precedent and undermine Congress’s judgment in the Westfall Act and the PLRA as to
the viability, scope, and substance of Carlson claims.
The Court should decline that invitation.
Nielsen argues that Watanabe’s claim is new because
he did not die. But  the survivorship claim in Carlson
necessarily depended on the premise that the decedent
could have asserted a claim had he survived. And in response to Carlson, Congress has not drawn the line at
death—the PLRA requires administrative exhaustion
for Carlson claims (something only a living plaintiff can
do) and makes physical injury, not death, the key metric
for obtaining damages. Requiring death for a Carlson
claim also overlooks that the Eighth Amendment is
meant to reduce suffering, and it would exempt officers
from damages liability even if they deliberately engage
in heinous conduct that causes extreme pain and injury
just short of death.
Nielsen additionally argues that other regulations or
statutes—most prominently, the Administrative Remedy Program (ARP) and the PLRA—render Watanabe’s
claim new. The ARP , though, is not even new: It was established in 1974, years before Carlson. And the ARP
introduces no new special factors not already addressed
in Carlson by the Court’s discussion of the Federal Tort
Claims Act (FTCA). The PLRA , for its part, confirms
that Congress views administrative remedies like the
ARP as a prerequisite, not a substitute, for a Carlson
claim. And if these factors are sufficient to render the
context here “new,” they would apply equally to and

4

foreclose all possible Carlson claims, dramatically undercutting Congress’s policy choices in the Westfall Act
and the PLRA.
Ultimately, Nielsen asks the Court to overrule
Bivens. But this is a Carlson case, and through the
Westfall Act and the PLRA, Congress has not just passively accepted Carlson—it has repeatedly legislated in
reliance on and in response to Carlson. This Court has
treated comparable congressional action as ratifying
other implied private rights of action. The Court should
do the same here. Having induced Congress’s action, the
Court should not eliminate the premise for that legislation nearly 50 years later.
The ordinary stare decisis factors also strongly counsel in favor of retaining Carlson. Though Carlson would
likely be decided differently today, it was not egregiously
wrong. The case followed a long history of damages
claims against federal officers and jailers specifically,
arising out of the fact that prisoners are wholly dependent on their jailers for their most basic needs. Congress
has relied on Carlson and its progeny to eliminate traditional state common-law remedies and to adjust the
procedures for Carlson claims. And Carlson is workable
and has worked for decades: It is supported by a robust
body of substantive case law and is limited by qualified
immunity. By contrast, overruling Carlson would create
a novel situation, never contemplated by Congress, in
which federal prisoners who are subjected to needless
suffering in violation of the Eighth Amendment have no
recourse against the responsible officers.
Separation of powers means that Carlson should not
be extended to new contexts. But those same principles
favor deference to Congress’s judgment in the Westfall

5

Act and the PLRA about the viability and scope of Carlson claims. Redefining Carlson to comprise a “null
set”—or overruling Carlson outright—would subordinate Congress’s policy determinations and undermine
the premise upon which Congress has legislated. The
decision should be affirmed.
CONSTITUTIONAL AND STATUTORY PROVISIONS
INVOLVED
Relevant statutory provisions, as well as a Bureau of
Prisons (BOP) administrative policy, are reproduced in
the appendix to this brief. App., infra, 1a-13a.
STATEMENT
A. Legal Background
1. Carlson and constitutional claims for damages
At the Founding, “the traditional way in which civil
litigation addressed abusive conduct” by federal officials
“was by subjecting them to liability for common -law
torts.” Hernandez v. Mesa, 589 U.S. 93, 110 (2020); see
also Pet. Br. 4. Although federal officers were generally
immune from such tort suits, that immunity dissolved
if the challenged conduct violated the Constitution. Pet.
Br. 4-5; Butz v. Economou, 438 U.S. 478, 489-91 (1978).
Beginning with Bivens v. Six Unknown Named
Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics , 403 U.S. 388
(1971), this Court recognized a federal, constitutional
analog for those traditional common-law claims in three
contexts. In Bivens, the Court permitted a plaintiff to
seek damages from federal narcotics agents for an unreasonable search in violation of the Fourth Amendment. Id. at 397. In Davis v. Passman, the Court permitted a congressional staffer to seek damages for sex

6

discrimination in violation of the Fifth Amendment. 442
U.S. 228, 248-49 (1979).
The following year, in Carlson v. Green, the Court
recognized a damages remedy for a federal prisoner alleging that prison officials were deliberately indifferent
to his serious medical needs in violation of the Eighth
Amendment. 446 U.S. 14 , 18-23 (1980). Carlson concerned allegations that a federal prison nurse and other
officials failed to provide medical care to inmate Joseph
Jones for his asthma. Id. at 16 n.1; Green v. Carlson, 581
F.2d 669, 670-71 (7th Cir. 1978). The complaint alleged
that this neglect caused Jones’s death, and his mother,
as administratrix of his estate, sued. Carlson, 446 U.S.
at 16 & n.1.
The Court held that a damages remedy was available
for the alleged violation of Jones’s Eighth Amendment
rights based on federal prison officials’ “deliberate[] indifferen[ce] to [his] serious medical needs.” Id. at 16 n.1,
18-23. The Court found no “special factors” counseling
hesitation, explaining that qualified immunity “provides adequate protection” against any inhibition of the
prison officials’ “efforts to perform their official duties.”
Id. at 19. The Court further explained that the FTCA,
28 U.S.C. 1346(b) and 2671-2680, did not displace any
implied constitutional claim. The Court found “no explicit congressional declaration” that persons injured by
federal officers’ violations of the Eighth Amendment
“may not recover money damages from the agents but
must be remitted to another remedy, equally effective in
the view of Congress,” and further found that the FTCA
is an inadequate substitute for a direct damages claim
against the individual officer. Carlson, 446 U.S. at 19-
23.

7

After recognizing a damages action, the Court separately held that the “action survived Jones’ death.” Id.
at 23. Because Bivens actions are creatures of federal
law, the Court adopted a uniform federal rule allowing
an action to survive when the defendant’ s conduct
causes the claimant’s death and state law would otherwise abate the claim. Id. at 23-25.
Since Carlson, this Court has “consistently refused to
extend Bivens liability to any new context.” Corr. Servs.
Corp. v. Malesko, 534 U.S. 61, 68 (2001). At the same
time, though, it has continued to identify Bivens, Davis,
and Carlson as “settled law” within their recognized
spheres, see Ziglar v. Abbasi, 582 U.S. 120, 134 (2017);
see, e.g., Goldey v. Fields, 606 U.S. 942, 942 (2025) (per
curiam) (referring to three “recognized … contexts” for
“implied Bivens causes of action”); Egbert v. Boule, 596
U.S. 482, 491 (2022) (Court has declined to “dispense
with Bivens”). In Abbasi, the Court emphasized that its
modern hesitation against extension of Bivens is “not intended to cast doubt on the continued force, or even the
necessity, of Bivens in the … context in which it arose.”
582 U.S. at 134.
Thus, “rather than dispense with Bivens altogether,”
Egbert, 596 U.S. at 491, the Court now applies a “twostep test” to determine whether a plaintiff states a
claim, Goldey, 606 U.S. at 944. A t step one, the Court
asks whether the claim is different in a “meaningful
way” from Bivens, Davis, or Carlson and therefore presents “a new Bivens context.” Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 139.
The non-exhaustive considerations at step one include
the officer’s rank, the constitutional right at issue, the
generality or specificity of the challenged action, the extent of judicial guidance, the legal mandate under which

8

the officer acted, the risk of disruptive intrusion into another branch, and potential “special factors” not considered in prior Bivens cases. Id. at 139-40.
If (and only if) the context is new, the Court proceeds
to the second step: whether there are “‘special factors’
indicating that the Judiciary is at least arguably less
equipped than Congress to ‘weigh the costs and benefits
of allowing a damages action to proceed.’” Egbert, 596
U.S. at 492 (quoting Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 136). The answer at step two, this Court has clarified, will almost always be that Congress is better equipped to determine
whether a plaintiff has a private right of action. See id.
at 491-92.
2. Legislative developments since Carlson
In 1988, Congress enacted the Federal Employees Liability Reform and Tort Compensation Act of 1988
(Westfall Act), Pub. L. No. 100-694, 102 Stat. 4563. The
Act generally makes the FTCA remedy “exclusive” for
common-law tort claims arising within the scope of federal employment. 28 U.S.C. 2679(b)(1) and (d)(1). But
that preemption “does not extend or apply” to a civil action against a federal employee “brought for a violation
of the Constitution.” 28 U.S.C. 2679(b)(2)(A). The Court
has since described th is provision as “[t] he Westfall
Act’s explicit exception for Bivens claims.” Hui v. Castaneda, 559 U.S. 799, 807 (2010).
Then, in 1996, Congress passed the PLRA, Pub. L.
No. 104 -134, 110 Stat. 1321 -66. Responding to this
Court’s decision in McCarthy v. Madigan holding that
Carlson plaintiffs need not exhaust administrative remedies, 503 U.S. 140, 156 (1992), the PLRA provides that
“[n]o action shall be brought with respect to prison conditions under section 1983 of this title, or any other Federal law,” until “such administrative remedies as are

9

available are exhausted.” 42 U.S.C. 1997e(a). The Court
has confirmed this provision applies to Bivens actions.
See Porter v. Nussle, 534 U.S. 516, 524 (2002).  The
PLRA also provides that “[n]o Federal civil action may
be brought” by a prisoner “for mental or emotional injury suffered while in custody without a prior showing
of physical injury.” 42 U.S.C. 1997e(e).
B. Factual Background1
On July 12, 2021, while incarcerated at Federal Detention Center (FDC) Honolulu, respondent Kekai
Watanabe was “brutally assaulted” by a group of inmates using an improvised weapon known as a “lock in
a sock.” Pet. App. 2a-4a, 21a, 25a, 42a, 57a (quotation
marks omitted). Federal prison officials documented his
“known and visible injuries,” and Watanabe was sent to
a solitary confinement unit. Id. at 4a. He remained
there for more than two months. Ibid.
On the evening of the attack, Watanabe asked to see
medical staff and reported “severe pain and headaches”
to two correctional officers. Id. at 4a, 25a, 42a. Several
days later, Watanabe was seen by petitioner Francis
Nielsen, a staff nurse at FDC Honolulu. Id. at 4a.
Watanabe informed Nielsen that he was “experiencing
severe back pain,” rating that pain as a “10” on a tenpoint scale. Ibid. When Watanabe requested treatment
at a hospital, Nielsen refused, telling him, “[y]ou are not
going to” the hospital and to “stop being a cry baby.”
Ibid.

1 Because this case arises on a motion to dismiss a pro se complaint, the facts alleged in the complaint are assumed to be true and
construed liberally in Watanabe’s favor. See Erickson v. Pardus,
551 U.S. 89, 94 (2007) (per curiam).

10

Watanabe repeatedly requested medical attention
and filed grievances through administrative channels.
Id. at 4a, 26a, 43a. During his more than two months in
solitary confinement and beyond, Watanabe was not
taken to a hospital or examined by a specialist; he received only intermittent and short-term treatment for
pain, often over-the-counter medication. Id. at 2a, 4a,
26a, 43a.
In February 2022, roughly seven months after the injury, an x-ray revealed that Watanabe had a fractured
coccyx and that bone chips had migrated into the surrounding soft tissue. Id. at 4a. Although prison officials
agreed to allow Watanabe to receive treatment from a
specialist, that never happened. Id. at 4a & n.3.
Watanabe was released from federal custody in 2024.
He remains in tremendous pain today.
C. Procedural History
Watanabe commenced this suit pro se in the United
States District Court for the District of Hawaii  on
March 31, 2022, seeking monetary damages and injunctive relief against Nielsen and other officials for violation of his Eighth Amendment rights. Pet. App. 5a, 42a-
43a. The district court granted Nielsen’s motion to dismiss, holding that Watanabe lacked a cause of action
under Carlson because his claim purportedly arose in a
new context. Id. at 24a-39a.
The Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded. Id. at 7a,
17a. The panel held at step one that the claim does not
present a new context because it does not meaningfully
differ from Carlson. Id. at 8a-16a. Applying the “non-exhaustive” considerations identified in Abbasi, the panel
found Watanabe’s claim mirrors the claim in Carlson in
every material respect. Id. at 8a-10a (citation omitted).
The panel rejected the district court’s finding that the

11

“nature and severity” of Watanabe’s claim meaningfully
differed from Carlson. Id. at 10a -14a. Noting that
Watanabe alleged a failure to respond to a “serious medical need” for seven months, resulting in “extreme pain,”
the panel held that “[a] plaintiff need not suffer death or
a life-threatening injury” to fall within Carlson. Id. at
13a-14a. The panel also held that the ARP “does not render this case a new context.” Id. at 14a-15a.
The Ninth Circuit denied panel rehearing and rehearing en banc. Id. at 77a.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
I. Watanabe’s claim arises in the same context as
Carlson: It is a damages action against a federal prison
officer who was deliberately indifferent to a federal prisoner’s serious medical needs in violation of the Eighth
Amendment. Watanabe suffered a broken bone , reported his extreme (ten out of ten) pain to a federal
prison officer (Nielsen), was deliberately denied medical
care for his condition for months, and endured needless
suffering as a result. The claim in Carlson concerned the
same kind of violation of the same constitutional right
by the same kind of defendant in the same kind of federal institution under the same legal framework. Differences in the precise medical condition—inherent in any
case—do not create a new context for application of
Carlson. They are case-specific, factual variations to
which that settled rule applies.
Nielsen and the United States resist this conclusion
by raising a series of “new context” arguments. But
every factor they identify was present in Carlson, is not
“meaningful[ly]” different from the facts at issue  in
Carlson, or has been considered and weighed by Congress. Indeed, Nielsen and the government largely overlook that Congress has actively legislated to preserve

12

and define Carlson claims, through the Westfall Act and
the PLRA. Nielsen’s arguments, if accepted, would subvert Congress’s policy choices and thus undermine, rather than advance, the separation of powers.
Nielsen argues that this case is different because
Watanabe survived while the victim in Carlson did not.
But the Court recognized a survivorship claim in Carlson only after determining that  the decedent would
have had a claim had he survived. And in response to
McCarthy, Congress determined in the PLRA that Carlson plaintiffs must first exhaust administrative remedies (an impossibility for deceased prisoners) and that
only physical injury, not death, is required for a prisoner
to recover most damages. Nielsen likewise asserts that
it is not “damages or nothing” for Watanabe, but that is
incorrect—damages are the only remedy Watanabe has
for his past pain and suffering.
Nielsen next offers several statutes and regulations,
including the ARP, that he says render the context new.
But the ARP is not new —it was in place years before
Carlson. And neither the ARP nor any of the statutes
Nielsen cites alters Carlson’s analysis of alternative
remedies. Moreover, Congress in the PLRA specifically
considered the interplay between Carlson and the ARP,
determining that the ARP should be a prerequisite to a
Carlson claim, not a complete bar.
II. What Nielsen and the United States really seek is
the end of Carlson, reducing those claims to a “null set.”
But they fail to justify that request under stare decisis.
Congress could have overruled Carlson at any time—
and it in fact has abrogated Davis and has limited Carlson. But Congress has elected not to overrule Carlson.
To the contrary, through legislation that “touch[es]
upon the implied right of action”—the Westfall Act and

13

the PLRA—Congress has “ratified the implied right of
action after the Court moved away from a broad willingness to imply private rights of action.” Stoneridge Inv.
Partners, LLC v. Sci.-Atlanta, Inc., 552 U.S. 148, 164
(2008). It would therefore upset Congress’s judgment to
subsequently overrule the precedent that provides the
foundation for that legislation.
The traditional stare decisis framework confirms as
much. Carlson was not egregiously wrong . Claims
against jailers for breach of their duty to provide for the
necessities of life have a long common -law tradition.
This Court has also long recognized that federal common law still exists within certain, discrete federal enclaves. The damages liability of a federal officer in a federally operated facility for violating duties arising out of
a federal conviction at least arguably fits within such an
enclave. The reliance interests here also are significant,
because overruling Carlson would alter the premise for
Congress’s subsequent actions. Finally, Carlson has not
proven unworkable, and overruling it would eliminate a
longstanding remedy for and deterrent against the deliberate imposition of unnecessary suffering on prisoners wholly dependent on federal officers.
This Court should affirm.
ARGUMENT
I. Watanabe’s Claim Arises In The Same Context As
Carlson
Even as this Court has “consistently refused to extend Bivens liability to any new context,” Malesko, 534
U.S. at 68, it has reaffirmed that Bivens and Carlson
remain settled law within their respective contexts, Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 134; Egbert, 596 U.S. at 490-92; Goldey,

14

606 U.S. at 944-45. Watanabe’s claim arises in that context.
A. Watanabe’s Claim Tracks Carlson In Every
Material Respect
This Court in Abbasi articulated “[t]he proper test for
determining whether a case presents a new Bivens context.” 582 U.S. at 139. “If the case is different in a meaningful way from previous Bivens cases decided by this
Court, then the context is new.” Ibid. The Court has
never exhaustively identified the factors that may give
rise to a new context, but it identified several potentially
relevant differences in Abbasi, including “the constitutional right at issue” and “the extent of judicial guidance
as to how an officer should respond.” Id. at 140.
With respect to Carlson specifically, this Court has
found a difference “meaningful” where a claim involved
different rights, different defendants, or new political
ramifications. For example, a Carlson claim does not lie
when it would entail “an inquiry into sensitive issues of
national security.” Id. at 142, 147-49. Nor can a claim be
brought against a privately operated prison or its employees. Malesko, 534 U.S. at 71-72; Minneci v. Pollard,
565 U.S. 118, 120 (2012). And entirely different types of
Eighth Amendment claims, such as ones based on excessive force, also fall outside Carlson’s medical-treatment context. See Goldey, 606 U.S. at 943-44.
Watanabe’s claim arises in the same context as Carlson. Watanabe was a federal prisoner in a federally operated prison, experienced a serious medical injury
(fractured bone with fragments that ultimately migrated into his tissue), was subjected to extreme pain
because of a nurse-level officer’s deliberate indifference,
and seeks damages for that violation of his Eighth

15

Amendment rights. The case thus involves the same officer rank; the same constitutional right; the same specificity of the official action; the same extent of judicial
guidance; and the same (or less) risk of disruptive intrusion. Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 139-40. There are no national
security issues, cf. Egbert, 596 U.S. at 494-96; Hernandez, 589 U.S. at 107-09; Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 142-43, and
the defendant is a federal officer, not a private ly-run
prison or employee thereof, cf. Minneci, 565 U.S. at 120;
Malesko, 534 U.S. at 63.
Watanabe’s claim also comports with how this Court
has repeatedly described Carlson’s scope. In Carlson,
the Court described the claim as involving federal
prison officials who were “deliberately indifferent to [a
prisoner’s] serious medical needs.” 446 U.S. at 16 n.1. In
Abbasi, the Court likewise characterized Carlson as “allow[ing] a Bivens claim for prisoner mistreatment—specifically, for failure to provide medical care.” 582 U.S. at
147. In Egbert, the Court described Carlson as recognizing a cause of action “for a federal prisoner’s inadequatecare claim under the Eighth Amendment.” 596 U.S. at
490-91. In Minneci, the Court described Carlson as permitting recovery from “personnel employed by the government” for Eighth Amendment violations involving
inadequate medical care. 565 U.S. at 126; see also
Malesko, 534 U.S. at 72 (when “a federal prisoner in a
BOP facility alleges a constitutional deprivation, he
may bring a Bivens claim against the offending individual officer”). And in McCarthy, the Court described the
claim as asserting that federal prison officials “had violated [a prisoner’s] constitutional rights under the
Eighth Amendment by their deliberate indifference to
his needs and medical condition.” 503 U.S. at 142. This
case arises in that same context.

16

This Court’s past description of Carlson’s scope is especially material because Congress has twice legislated
in response to Carlson. In the Westfall Act,  Congress
preempted essentially all state tort suits  for money
damages against federal officers for conduct undertaken
in their official capacity and made FTCA claims against
the United States the exclusive damages remedies for
such torts. See 28 U.S.C. 2679(b). But Congress was
careful to carve out actions “brought for a violation of
the Constitution of the United States.” 28 U.S.C.
2679(b)(2)(A). This Court has understood that provision
as “[t]he Westfall Act’s explicit exception for Bivens
claims.” Hui, 559 U.S. at 807.
Congress further built around Carlson and its progeny specifically, through the PLRA. In McCarthy, the
Court held that a federal prisoner pursuing a Carlson
claim for deliberate indifference to a serious medical
condition need not  exhaust administrative remedies
(i.e., the ARP) before filing a claim in federal court. 503
U.S. at 156. After concluding that no existing exhaustion statute applied, the Court found no “special factors”
that would require exhaustion of the ARP before pursuing a Carlson claim. Id. at 151-52.
Congress thereafter enacted the PLRA, which abrogated McCarthy and now requires all prisoners (state or
federal) to exhaust “such administrative remedies as
are available” before any action may be brought “under
section 1983 … or any other Federal law .” 42 U.S.C.
1997e(a). As this Court has recognized, that is properly
understood as a response to McCarthy. See Booth v.
Churner, 532 U.S. 731, 739-41 (2001) (“[T]he fair inference to be drawn is that Congress meant to preclude the
McCarthy result.”); Nussle, 534 U.S. at 527-28. In the
PLRA, Congress also limited the availability of mental

17

or emotional damages to those circumstances in which
a prisoner also suffers physical  injury. 42 U.S.C.
1997e(e).
The Westfall Act and the PLRA together represent
Congress’s measured judgment about the existence and
boundaries of Carlson claims. Nielsen urges that Congress is best positioned to “balanc[e]” the costs and benefits of a damages action. See Pet. Br. 22, 31, 41. The
United States echoes that “Congress possesses the authority and competence to balance the benefits of a damages remedy against the risk of abusive litigation.” U.S.
Br. 14. But Congress has exercised that authority and
indicated its view that Carlson claims remain available
within their existing context, subject to the procedural
and substantive limitations defined in the PLRA.
Nielsen cites this Court’s observation in Hernandez
that the Westfall Act merely “left Bivens where it found
it.” 589 U.S. at 111 n.9; Pet. Br. 46-47. Exactly so. And
Congress did not, in 1988, find Bivens (and Carlson) as
a “null set.” U.S. Br. 25. Rather, when Congress passed
the Westfall Act, this Court had repeatedly described
Carlson as allowing a claim “under the Eighth Amendment’s proscription against cruel and unusual punishment.” United States v. Stanley, 483 U.S. 669, 678
(1987); Schweiker v. Chilicky, 487 U.S. 412, 421 (1988)
(action permitted “under … the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause”). For purposes of the new context
analysis, the passage of the Westfall Act confirms Congress’s view that Carlson claims should continue to exist
in their original context. This case arises in that context.
B. There Is No New Context
In response, Nielsen and the government point to a
combination of factors that (1) existed in Carlson, (2) are
not “meaningful[ly]” different from those analyzed in

18

Carlson, and/or (3) have since been considered and legislated on by Congress.
1. Differences in the severity, timing, and outcome of
a medical episode do not give rise to a new context
Purported differences in the “nature, severity, and
immediacy” between this case and Carlson do not give
rise to a new context. See Pet. Br. 24.
a. Nielsen does not dispute that Watanabe has alleged a serious medical injury but argues this case presents a new context because Watanabe, unlike the prisoner in Carlson, survived the violation of his Eighth
Amendment rights. See Pet. Br. 27 -29. Carlson forecloses that argument, as do the Eighth Amendment and
Congress’s policy judgments in the PLRA.
Carlson addressed two distinct, but related, issues.
First, the Court determined that a federal prisoner
whose Eighth Amendment rights are violated through
deliberate indifference to a serious medical need may
assert a damages claim for relief against the responsible
officer. Carlson, 446 U.S. at 16-23. Second, the Court determined that the decedent’s estate could assert that
claim under a federal common-law rule of survivorship.
Id. at 23-25.
The Court’s conclusion that the estate could assert a
survivorship claim necessarily depen ded on the first
holding that the decedent had a cause of action before
his death. That is because a survivorship claim is
“wholly derivative” of the decedent’s own claim—if the
victim would not have had a claim had he survived, then
the estate has no survivorship claim. Restatement
(Third) of Torts  § 71 ( A.L.I., Tentative Draft No. 3,
2024); see also Mich. Cent. R.R. Co. v. Vreeland, 227
U.S. 59, 67-68 (1913) (survival statutes preserve “the

19

right of action which the injured person might have
prosecuted if he had survived”).
Carlson therefore forecloses distinguishing claims
based on death or survival. “[I]t is not only the result but
also those portions of the opinion necessary to that result by which we are bound.” Seminole Tribe of Fla. v.
Florida, 517 U.S. 44, 67 (1996). And “necessary to [the]
result” in Carlson was the conclusion that the decedent,
had he survived, would have had a cause of action. Indeed, t he Court stated clearly that “the question
whether respondent’s action survived Jones’ death is a
question of federal law.” Carlson, 446 U.S. at 18 (emphasis added).
Nielsen’s proposed rule also is inconsistent with how
this Court has since interpreted Carlson. The Court
held in Davis that “[w]hether petitioner has asserted a
cause of action … depends not on the quality or extent of
her injury, but on whether the class of litigants of which
petitioner is a member may use the courts to enforce the
right at issue.” Davis, 442 U.S. at 239 n.18 (emphasis
added). In Abbasi, the Court observed that the plaintiffs’
injuries there—which did not result in death —were
“just as compelling as those at issue in Carlson.” 582
U.S. at 147. And the Court has described Carlson as giving the prisoner—not his estate—a cause of action for
damages. See Malesko, 534 U.S. at 72 (“If a federal prisoner in a BOP facility alleges a constitutional deprivation, he may bring a Bivens claim against the offending
individual officer.”). Nielsen’s contention that “death is
different” conflicts with that precedent.
Congress has affirmed this understanding of Carlson. In the PLRA, Congress responded to McCarthy by
requiring exhaustion of administrative remedies like

20

the ARP before pursuing a Carlson claim. Congress necessarily contemplated that living prisoners like McCarthy would be pursuing those claims: The PLRA applies
only to actions brought by a prisoner , 42 U.S.C.
1997e(a), and only living prisoners or ex-prisoners can
use the ARP. Congress also defined the types of injuries
for which a prisoner may recover damages—prisoners
may not recover damages for an emotional or mental injury absent an underlying physical injury . 42 U.S.C.
1997e(e). It could have instead drawn the line between
surviving and deceased plaintiffs—but it did not, even
though it was responding to a Carlson case in which the
plaintiff was alive.
Nielsen and the United States cite various statutes
in which Congress has provided for remedies when
death results. See Pet. Br. 27-28; U.S. Br. 23 & n.1. But
most of those statutes only enhance the remedy available if death ensues—they do not make the existence of a
remedy dependent on death. See, e.g., 5 U.S.C. 8102 and
8102a; 33 U.S.C. 908 and 909. Nielsen and the United
States identify no statute in which there is a substantive
violation but no damages unless death occurs. Cf. 46
U.S.C. 30302 (Death on the High Seas Act imposing
both liability and damages only for death). In any event,
if Congress wanted to choose death as the dividing line
for Carlson claims, it could have done so in the PLRA—
it did not.
Finally, Nielsen’s distinction is fundamentally backward as a matter of Eighth Amendment  law. The
Eighth Amendment does not protect against death itself—it protects against “tortures and barbarous punishments” that intensify punishment “with a (cruel) superaddition of terror, pain, or disgrace.” Bucklew v.

21

Precythe, 587 U.S. 119, 131, 133 (2019) (alteration, citations, and quotation marks omitted). It is the suffering,
not death itself, that violates the Eighth Amendment.
Correspondingly, damages in a survivorship claim are
available only for the suffering incurred up to the point
of death. See 1 Jacob A. Stein, Stein on Personal Injury
Damages § 3:53 (3d ed. 2026). That accords with the traditional rule that “by the common law no civil action lies
for an injury which results in death.” Mobile Life Ins.
Co. v. Brame, 95 U.S. 754, 756 (1877). If anything, Nielsen’s rule inverts the Eighth Amendment (and the common law) by imposing liability on officers who (through
their deliberate indifference) cause a painful but quick
death, while absolving those who deliberately prolong
suffering.
b. Nielsen also argues that Watanabe’s case arises
in a new context because it is not “damages or nothing”
for him and he did not suffer an “acute and fatal medical
emergency.” Pet. Br. 25 -27. Those arguments fail on
both the law and the facts.
Only damages can compensate for past pain and suffering—the crux of a Carlson claim. See Carlson, 446
U.S. at 20-21. “The sole function of an … injunction is to
forestall future violations”; that remedy is “unrelated to
… reparations” for the past pain and suffering caused
by the violation of Eighth Amendment rights. See
United States v. Or. State Med. Soc’y, 343 U.S. 326, 333
(1952). In Abbasi, the Court distinguished between
cases that involved “individual instances of discrimination or law enforcement overreach, which due to their
very nature are difficult to address except by way of
damages actions after the fact,” and cases challenging
“large-scale policy decisions” that affect “hundreds of

22

prisoners” and are more effectively addressed by injunctive relief. 582 U.S. at 144. Neither in Carlson nor any
other decision has the Court indicated that a Carlson
remedy is available only if the plaintiff could not also or
alternatively seek injunctive relief.
Congress endorsed this view in the PLRA. There,
Congress set strict limits on the type and scope of injunctive relief courts could afford prisoners. 18 U.S.C.
3626(a)(1)-(3). And it separately limited the circumstances in which a prisoner may recover for emotional
or mental injury. 42 U.S.C. 1997e(e). But nowhere did it
suggest that the availability of injunctive relief acts as a
bar against damages —the PLRA contemplates both
forms of relief. And the PLRA did not alter the traditional rule that injunctive relief is the exception, available only where there is no adequate remedy at law. See
eBay Inc. v. MercExchange, LLC, 547 U.S. 388, 391
(2006). So long as the injury is not purely mental or emotional, a prisoner may recover damages.
Nielsen’s “damages or nothing” argument also would
render the PLRA’s exhaustion requirement largely
meaningless in the precise context in which it was intended to apply. The PLRA requires exhaustion of administrative remedies before a federal prisoner may
pursue a Carlson claim, which can take months (or
longer). But in fleeting emergencies, administrative
remedies are not practically available and need not be
exhausted. Cf. Ross v. Blake, 578 U.S. 632, 643-44, 648
(2016). Thus, under Nielsen’s rule, the only viable Carlson claims are those that do not require exhaustion.
That would make Congress’s choice to add an administrative exhaustion requirement for Carlson claims essentially meaningless and render Congress’s response

23

to McCarthy largely moot. Indeed, the plaintiff in
McCarthy himself would have no claim.
Nielsen’s related argument distinguishing claims
based on whether they are sufficiently “acute” additionally invites courts to make the precise kinds of policy
judgments he argues are inappropriate. See Pet. Br. 22-
26. That proposed distinction reflects a policy judgment
to allow a cause of action for deliberate indifference to
only some (but not all) serious medical needs. And
whether an injury is “acute” or “chronic” is fluid and illdefined. For example, the victim i n Carlson was a
“chronic asthmatic” and was denied medical treatment
for days before the final episode that led to his death.
See Green, 581 F.2d at 671. Likewise, a fractured coccyx,
like that here, results in both immediate pain and longterm injury. See Gustav Ø. Andersen et al., Coccydynia—The Efficacy of Available Treatment Options: A
Systematic Review, 12 Glob. Spine J. 1611, 1612 (2022).
A court is ill-equipped at the pleading stage to categorize these injuries as “acute” or “chronic.”  And once
again, Congress has not required an acute injury; it
simply requires physical injury. The severity of the injury goes to the merits, not the existence of a cause of
action.
Finally, it is, for all intents and purposes, “damages
or nothing” for Watanabe. Watanabe was kept in solitary confinement for two months following the injury.
Watanabe eventually did pursue an administrative
remedy and did seek injunctive relief. But those requests were stalled for years, and Watanabe has now
been released from federal custody. Thus, for Watanabe,
it is damages or nothing—if his case is dismissed, he has
no redress for his past suffering, and he cannot get an
injunction because he was released. That is not unusual

24

in the Carlson context—federal prisoners are often
transferred or released before the administrative or judicial process is complete. See, e.g., Joseph Shapiro &
Christie Thompson, ‘Rejected’: How Federal Prisons
Stonewall Grievances and Deny Care for Years , NPR
(June 17, 2026 ), https://www.wlrn.org/npr-breakingnews/2026-06-17/rejected-how-federal-prisons-stonewall-grievances-and-deny-care-for-years (describing
long resolution time for administrative grievances).
2. The ARP and other remedies do not distinguish
this case from Carlson
Nielsen additionally contends that various alternative statutory or regulatory schemes—primarily the
ARP—give rise to a new context here. See Pet. Br. 32-
38. They do not.
a. Nielsen relies first on the ARP, a four-step administrative grievance scheme that governs federal prisons.
See Pet. Br. 10, 32-33. For several reasons, the ARP does
not create a new context.
First, the ARP grievance procedure was in place at
the time of Carlson and thus is not even a “difference.”
Nielsen argues that the ARP was not adopted until
1979, after the underlying injury in Carlson. See id. at
38; see also U.S. Br. 17 (asserting the BOP “created its
[ARP]” in “1979”). That is incorrect: The BOP—under
the leadership of Norman Carlson, a named defendant
in Carlson—created its administrative remedy procedure in 1974, with substantially the same four-step process that exists today. See U.S. Dep’t of Just., Bureau of
Prisons, Policy Statement No. 2001.6A (Oct. 18, 1974).
In 1976, Chief Justice Burger praised Carlson for developing “simple, workable internal procedures to deal
with prisoner complaints.” Chief Justice Burger Issues
Year[-]end Report, 62 A.B.A.J. 189-90 (Feb. 1976).

25

In 1979, the BOP formally codified its existing policy
as part of a broader project to publicize the policies
“presently contained in Policy Statements and Operations Memoranda.” 42 Fed. Reg. 26,334 (May 23, 1977);
see also 42 Fed. Reg. 64,082 (Dec. 21, 1977) (notice of
proposed rulemaking for the “third installment” of that
effort, including the ARP). That codification did not alter the substance of the ARP, which already existed and
was well known. And regardless whether the victim in
Carlson or his family could actually have used the ARP,
what matters for Bivens is the existence of the remedy
for this type of claim, irrespective of its effectiveness or
availability to any particular plaintiff. See Goldey, 606
U.S. at 944-45; Egbert, 596 U.S. at 493.
Second, the Court’s decision in Carlson necessarily
forecloses relying on the ARP as a new factor. In Carlson, the Court discussed the availability of alternative
remedies, including the FTCA, to determine whether
the plaintiff had an implied private right of action. 446
U.S. at 19-23. The Court concluded the FTCA does not
foreclose a constitutional claim for damages, including
because the statute does not provide for liability against
individual officers, does not allow for punitive damages,
and does not allow for a jury trial. Ibid. That same analysis applies to the ARP, which has the same shortcomings as the FTCA and does not allow for damages. Indeed, when Congress enacted the Westfall Act, the ARP
did not allow for tort claims . 28 C.F.R. 542.12 (1987).
And today, the ARP directs the BOP to “refer the inmate
to the appropriate statutorily-mandated procedures”—
namely, the FTCA. 28 C.F.R. 542.10(c). The ARP therefore channels those claims into the very statutory
scheme that Carlson analyzed and found insufficient.

26

Relying on Egbert, Nielsen argues that Carlson’s
FTCA analysis “carries little weight” under the Court’s
current approach. Pet. Br. 38-39 (quoting Egbert, 596
U.S. at 500-01). But that misses the point. Watanabe
does not seek to extend Carlson’s analysis to a new context, because the Court’s analysis in Carlson regarding
the FTCA necessarily subsumes the lesser remedy of
the ARP and forecloses the arguments Nielsen now
raises.
This Court’s decisions have also implicitly rejected
the notion that the ARP creates a new context. In
Malesko, the Court expressly acknowledged the ARP as
a remedial mechanism available to federal prisoners,
534 U.S. at 74, but also reaffirmed that a prisoner in a
BOP facility may sue the offending officer under Carlson, id. at 72. In Abbasi, the Court found a new context
based on profound differences involving confinement of
noncitizens in the national security context, without so
much as mentioning the ARP as a distinguishing factor.
582 U.S. at 140. And in Goldey, the Court considered the
ARP only at step two, after concluding that the excessive-force claim there arose in a new context. 606 U.S.
at 944. The analysis in those cases would be superfluous, incorrect, or both if Nielsen were correct.
Third, Nielsen’s argument would subvert Congress’s
policy choices. When Congress passed the Westfall Act
in 1988, it was legislating in light of the analysis in Carlson, which concluded that alternative remedies like the
FTCA did not displace a constitutional claim. Congress
thus would not have reasonably expected that the Court
would deem the ARP—already in place at the time of
Carlson—as prohibitive of a Carlson claim.
Later, Congress itself addressed the ARP directly in
the PLRA. Responding to McCarthy, Congress made the

27

ARP a prerequisite to a Carlson claim rather than a substitute. 42 U.S.C. 1997e(a). Congress therefore has already defined the role the ARP plays vis-à-vis Carlson
claims and determined it does not bar such claims. Foreclosing Carlson claims on the basis of the ARP would
upend Congress’s judgment in the PLRA about the significance of the ARP  in this exact species of prisoner
claims.
b. Nielsen next invokes the PLRA as a new context,
see Pet. Br. 33, but the PLRA supports, rather than refutes, the existence of a cognizable Carlson claim here.
As Nielsen acknowledges, “the PLRA gave Congress
‘specific occasion to consider the matter of prisoner
abuse and to consider the proper way to remedy those
wrongs.’” Ibid. (quoting Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 148); see
also U.S. Br. 16 (similar). And one of Congress’s express
goals was to curb the maintenance of “frivolous” or “malicious” prisoner claims. 42 U.S.C. 1997e(c); see also
Nussle, 534 U.S. at 524 (PLRA was passed with the intent “to reduce the quantity and improve the quality of
prisoner suits”). Yet rather than eliminate Carlson
claims altogether—a path it largely followed with Davis
and that surely would have reduced the risk of frivolous
or malicious claims—Congress chose instead to define
the procedural and substantive limits of Carlson claims.
Nielsen points to the omission of an express damages
cause of action in the PLRA. Pet. Br. 33. But Congress
had no need to create a Carlson cause of action in the
PLRA, because it already existed. See Abbasi, 582 U.S.
at 148-49; McCarthy, 503 U.S. at 151. Congress likewise
had no need to create a cause of action for injunctive relief—which the Court has long recognized —yet the
United States cites the PLRA as implicitly codifying
such a right. U.S. Br. 18. Instead, Congress legislated in

28

reliance on Carlson, operating on the assumption that
such claims existed, but modifying the procedural and
substantive limitations on those claims. Treating the
PLRA as a new context would defeat Congress’s careful
work.
c. Finally, Nielsen and the United States  offer a
handful of disparate statutes they say create a new context. See Pet. Br. 34-35; U.S. Br. 15-17. But those statutes are far afield.
The USA PATRIOT Act is a national-security statute
that generally directs a designated DOJ official to receive and review civil rights complaints against government officials. Pub. L. No. 107-56, § 1001, 115 Stat. 391
(2001). The Prison Rape Elimination Act seeks to “increase the accountability of prison officials who fail to
detect, prevent, reduce and punish prison rape.” 34
U.S.C. 30302(6). The statute cites Farmer v. Brennan,
511 U.S. 825 (1994) —a Carlson case—with approval.
See Pub. L. No. 108 -79, § 2(13), 117 Stat. 973 (2003).
Neither statute concerns prisoner claims for deliberate
indifference to a serious medical condition. And the Federal Prison Oversight Act was enacted after Watanabe’s

not. See Pub. L. No. 118-71, § 2(b), 138 Stat. 1501 (2024);
U.S. Br. 16-17; Pet. Br. 34-35 & n.13. The Act specifies
that none of its oversight mechanisms “shall be construed as a necessary administrative remedy required
for exhaustion under” the PLRA. § 2(a), 138 Stat. 1501.

undermine or alter Congress’s judgment in the Westfall
Act or the PLRA that Carlson claims remain cognizable
within their own sphere.  The government cites this
Court’s statement in Goldey that “Congress has actively

29

legislated in the area of prisoner litigation but has not
enacted a statutory cause of action for money damages.”
606 U.S. at 944; U.S. Br. 17. But that statement was
made in the context of a claim for excessive force. The
Court had no occasion to consider the existing cause of
action for deliberate indifference to a serious medical

C. Nielsen’s Rule Would Effectively Overrule Carlson
Ultimately, Nielsen and the United States do not
seek to limit Carlson to its context, but rather to eliminate the Carlson remedy while purporting to retain the
precedent in name only. They each invoke this Court’s
statement in Abbasi that “a case can present a new context … if there are potential special factors that were not
considered in previous Bivens cases.” 582 U.S. at 148.
They contend that a case arises in a new context if it
involves a factor the Court did not specifically “consider”
in the Bivens trilogy—even if the factor was present in
the cases, was analyzed in the case s, or has subsequently been addressed by Congress. See, e.g., Pet. Br.
18-19, 24, 32-35; U.S. Br. 15. As the United States concedes, this approach would render Carlson cases a “null
set.” U.S. Br. 24-25.
This application of the two-step framework would effectively overrule Carlson and thereby contravene Congress’s judgment in the Westfall Act to allow constitutional claims against federal officers within their existing context, notwithstanding the elimination of preexisting state common -law claims. It would transform
that statute from one that channels constitutional
claims through federal law into one that extinguishes
those claims altogether. Likewise, redefining the twostep framework to eliminate all possible Carlson claims

30

would disrupt the infrastructure for Carlson claims established through the PLRA.
That understanding of the Westfall Act and the
PLRA fully comports with Abbasi. Materially different
facts may lead to different outcomes. See, e.g., Cohens v.
Virginia, 19 U.S. (6 Wheat.) 264, 399 -400 (1821) (controlling portion of the opinion is that which resolves
“[t]he question actually before the Court”). That is what
happened in Abbasi—the Court distinguished the case
before it from Carlson on the ground that the case entailed a “different constitutional right” with “less developed” “guidance available to” the defendants. Abbasi,
582 U.S. at 148. It did not permit parties to avoid binding precedent simply by coming up with an argument a
previous litigant did not raise or by identifying an immaterial factual difference.
Indeed, to read Abbasi as Nielsen and the United
States propose would render Abbasi internally incoherent. See Holland v. Jackson, 542 U.S. 649, 654 (2004)
(per curiam) (rejecting a reading of a judicial opinion
that “would needlessly create internal inconsistency in
the opinion”). That is because even while the Court in
Abbasi determined that the claims before it raised a new
context, 582 U.S. at 147, it also reaffirmed that Carlson
(and Bivens) remain good law within their respective
spheres, id. at 131, 134. But if any new argument not
expressly discussed in Carlson gives rise to a new context, then every case is a new context—including the exact facts of Carlson—and Carlson in fact is not good law.
Put otherwise, Nielsen and the United States purport to
apply Abbasi at the same time they imply Abbasi was
wrong to suggest any Bivens claims remain. That is an
untenable reading of the precedent.

31

The extreme consequences of Nielsen’s and the government’s approach are apparent from their attempted
application of it. Nielsen argues that the ARP and the
PLRA establish a new context, but both are implicated
in every possible claim that could arise under Carlson.
See, e.g., Carrin v. Strong, 182 F.4th 1351, 1362 -63
(11th Cir. 2026) (finding a new context given the existence of the ARP notwithstanding that the inmate died
from his injury). The United States urges that the fact
that Watanabe was incarcerated at the time of his injury gives rise to a new context. Of course, Carlson also
arose in prison—the decedent’s conviction and imprisonment were the only reasons the Eighth Amendment
applied at all. See Ingraham v. Wright, 430 U.S. 651,
671 n.40 (1977). And the Court did consider the effect a
damages claim could have on officials’ “efforts to perform their official duties.” Carlson, 446 U.S. at 19. The
United States’ arguments are therefore no different
from saying that Carlson should be overruled.
Nielsen takes this argument one step further by urging that there is now only one step in the framework and
that a Carlson claim is foreclosed if there is any “‘rational reason to think’ Congress might be better suited”

492). But that approach is inconsistent with the two -
step framework, as it would eliminate the first step entirely, no longer requiring any difference (meaningful or
otherwise) from Carlson. The Court’s comment in Egbert that the two steps may sometimes resolve into one,
596 U.S. at 492, is better understood as observing that
if a case implicates a meaningful, new factor at step one,
then that same factor will likely foreclose extension of
Carlson at step two. But the Court confirmed in Egbert

32

that the two-step framework remains operative, id. at
494, 498-99, and it reaffirmed as much in Goldey, 606
U.S. at 944.
A decision that Carlson can never apply, even on its
own facts, is no different from overruling Carlson. See,
e.g., FEC v. Wisconsin Right to Life, 551 U.S. 449, 463
(2007) (it “would effectively overrule” a prior decision to

or so dramatically limit, earlier authority sub silentio.”
Shalala v. Ill. Council on Long Term Care, Inc., 529 U.S.
1, 18 (2000). Even in cases where the Court has deemed

33

II. The Court Should Not Overrule Carlson
Although their arguments would effectively overrule
Carlson, neither Nielsen nor the United States can justify that extraordinary request. Indeed, Nielsen does not
even ask to overrule Carlson: He focuses only on
whether Bivens should be overruled, Pet. Br. 42-48, but
as the government notes, this case is about Carlson, not
Bivens, U.S. Br. 23-28.
Stare decisis carries “special force” here, where Congress could displace Carlson if it chose. See Michigan v.
Bay Mills Indian Cmty., 572 U.S. 782, 799, 801 -03 &
n.12 (2014) (citation omitted); see also Kimble v. Marvel
Ent., LLC, 576 U.S. 446, 455 (2015). Overruling Carlson
would upend Congress’s careful judgment about the
types of remedies available to victims of constitutional
violations in federal prison and result in a scheme never
sanctioned or contemplated by Congress. And regardless of whether Carlson would be decided differently today, it was not “egregiously wrong.” NRSC, 146 S. Ct. at
2424 (citation omitted). Carlson claims arise in a federal
enclave and align with centuries of common-law precedent allowing private rights of action against jailers for
mistreatment.
The Court should instead reaffirm what it has said
for many years: Carlson is still good law within its own
context but should not be extended further. The Court’s
decision in Cisco Systems, Inc. v. Doe I provides an unusually close parallel. 146 S. Ct. 1882 (2026). After rejecting any power to define new torts under the Alien Tort
Statute, the Court reaffirmed that plaintiffs could still
proceed under the three torts long recognized at common law. See id. at 1892 n.3. “[T]o the extent there has
been reliance on the availability of those three actions,
we see no need to revisit them.” Ibid. “[W]e say ‘this far

34

and no further.’” Ibid. That is all the Court need do here
to rebuff Nielsen’s arguments.
A. Overruling Carlson Would Defy Separation of
Powers and Subvert Congressional Design
In the intervening decades since Carlson, Congress
has twice legislated to preserve, ratify, and provide infrastructure for Carlson claims. Overruling Carlson
now would subvert Congress’s intent and violate the
very separation-of-powers principles Nielsen advances.
1. Congress has ratified Carlson
When Congress enacted the Westfall Act, it extinguished the traditional remedy of using state common
law to hold individual federal officers liable in damages
for unconstitutional conduct undertaken in the course of
their duties. 28 U.S.C. 2679(b)(1). That remedy had existed all the way back to the Founding. See p. 5, supra.
But Congress eliminated that remedy only on the understanding that the constitutional claims recognized in
Bivens and Carlson would remain available. See 28
U.S.C. 2679(b)(2)(A); see also United States v. Smith,
499 U.S. 160, 173 (1991) (Westfall Act “preserv[ed] employee liability for Bivens actions”). The House Report
explained that “the courts have identified” torts that “violat[e] … one or more fundamental rights embraced in
the Constitution” as “a more serious intrusion of the
rights of an individual that merits special attention,”
and that a “major feature” of the Westfall Act “is that
the exclusive remedy expressly does not extend to so -
called constitutional torts. See Bivens v. Six Unknown
Agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388
(1971).” H.R. Rep. No. 100-700, 100th Cong., 2d Sess. 6
(1988).

35

In 1996, Congress passed the PLRA in further reliance on Carlson. As detailed above, the PLRA requires
exhaustion of administrative remedies  for prisoner
claims, 42 U.S.C. 1997e(a), a change that was made in
direct response to the decision in McCarthy. The PLRA
also expressly contemplates the existence of money
damages—no less so than the injunctive relief the government touts. See U.S. Br. 18-19.
2. Overruling Carlson would contravene Congress’s
ratification
The Court has consistently treated comparable legislative action as ratification of the underlying decision—
even when that decision recognized an implied right of
action that conflicts with modern jurisprudence.
a. Decades ago, the Court implied a private right of
action under Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange
Act of 1934. See Blue Chip Stamps v. Manor Drug
Stores, 421 U.S. 723, 730 (1975). Congress has never
amended the statute to expressly provide for such a
right of action, but in the Private Securities Litigation
Reform Act, Congress added heightened pleading requirements and a loss causation requirement for any
“private action” arising under the statute. 15 U.S.C.
78u-4(b). In Stoneridge, this Court observed that even
though it is now “settled that there is an implied cause
of action only if the underlying statute can be interpreted to disclose the intent to create one,” the amendments by Congress plainly “touch upon the implied right
of action” and therefore “ratified the implied right of action after the Court moved away from a broad willingness to imply private rights of action.” 552 U.S. at 164-
65 (emphasis added).
The Court offered a similar analysis in Alexander v.
Sandoval. There, the Court concluded that Congress

36

had “ratified” the Court’s creation in Cannon v. University of Chicago, 441 U.S. 677 (1979), of a private right of
action to enforce Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
and Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972. Alexander v. Sandoval, 532 U.S. 275, 280 (2001). Congress
did not explicitly endorse Cannon, but the Court understood subsequent enactments—those that “abrogated
States’ sovereign immunity against suits brought in federal court to enforce” Titles VI and IX, for example—to
“‘validat[e]’” Cannon. Id. at 280 (citation omitted).
Still again, in Bay Mills, the Court declined to abrogate precedent affording Native American tribes sovereign immunity for certain commercial activity because
Congress had “made an initial … decision to retain that
form of tribal immunity.” 572 U.S. at 801. But Congress
had not actually codified that immunity—it simply had
rejected proposed legislation modifying tribal immunity
in the commercial context and “chose to enact a far more
modest alternative.” Id. at 802. To overrule its prior
precedent following such congressional action, the
Court concluded, “would replace Congress’s considered
judgment with our contrary opinion.” Id. at 803.
Carlson is on even firmer footing. Just as it did with
other implied private rights of action, Congress legislated around Carlson to define the procedural framework that governs such claims. See 42 U.S.C. 1997e.
And just as it did with tribal immunity, Congress has
rejected efforts to overturn Carlson, see S. 1775, 97th
Cong. (1981); H.R. 7034, 97th Cong. (1982), and enacted
substantive limitations on Carlson claims, see 42 U.S.C.
1997e(e), but did not eliminate those claims entirely.
Congress has therefore “already reflected on an issue of”

37

federal officer liability and “declined to change settled
law.” Bay Mills, 572 U.S. at 803.2
The Westfall Act goes even further: It preempts virtually all state common-law tort claims against federal
employees for conduct undertaken in the scope of their
duties, but Congress went out of its way  to preserve
Carlson claims. The exclusivity provision in the Westfall
Act applies on its face to Bivens claims—to preserve
Bivens claims, Congress had to take the affirmative step
of excepting Bivens claims from the statutory bar that
would otherwise apply. To overturn Carlson now would
“replace Congress’s considered judgment with [the
Court’s] contrary opinion.” Ibid.
b. Nielsen does not address the ratification effect of
the PLRA and urges only briefly that the Westfall Act
left Bivens “in the hands of courts.” Pet. Br. 47. That is
an overstatement. Congress indeed “left Bivens where it
found it,” Hernandez, 589 U.S. at 111 n.9, but not by
leaving its ultimate fate to the Court. At the time of the
Westfall Act, Carlson claims were not a “null set,” U.S.
Br. 25, but rather a material and real means for prisoners to obtain monetary relief for Eighth Amendment violations. The Westfall Act represents a judgment by
Congress to preserve Carlson. That is not passive indifference—it is affirmative action ratifying this Court’s
decision. And the PLRA further ratifies Carlson by
erecting a procedural and substantive framework.

2  Nielsen notes that Congress has declined to pass different bills
that would create a sweeping analogue to Section 1983 for federal
officers. Pet. Br. 11-12, 47. That is weak evidence of congressional
intent. See Central Bank of Denver, N.A. v. First Interstate Bank of
Denver, N.A., 511 U.S. 164, 187 (1994) (failed proposals “deserve little weight in the interpretive process”).

38

Nielsen suggests, in a footnote, that perhaps Congress has not overruled Carlson because it mistakenly
believes it cannot do so. Pet. Br. 47 n.15. That is baseless. A principal question in Carlson was whether Congress had displaced a constitutional claim through the
FTCA. See 446 U.S. at 19-20. Then-Justice Rehnquist,
in dissent, made it a point to remind Congress that it
could overrule Carlson (and Bivens). Id. at 51 -53
(Rehnquist, J., dissenting). And Congress took note—it
has legislated to overrule Bivens cases, in whole or in
part. In 1995, Congress abrogated Davis in substantial
part by creating an exclusive statutory remedy for congressional-employment rights and protections through
the Congressional Accountability Act of 1995, Pub. L.
No. 104 -1, § 225(d)(1) , 109 Stat. 22. See 2 U.S.C.
1361(d)(1). Congress knows it could overrule Carlson,
but it has chosen to do the opposite.
Overruling Carlson or declaring it inapplicable in
every circumstance would intrude on Congress’s legislative judgment and “scale the heights of presumption.”
Bay Mills, 572 U.S. at 803. Whatever the foundations of
Carlson, it now bears the imprimatur of Congress.
B. The Ordinary Stare Decisis Factors Favor Carlson
The ordinary stare decisis factors further justify retaining Carlson. Those factors require the Court to assess “the egregiousness of the precedent’s error,” “any
cognizable reliance interests,” and “the jurisprudential
and real-world effects of the decision.” NRSC, 146 S. Ct.
at 2424.
1. Carlson was not egregiously wrong
Carlson would likely come out differently if decided
today. But “ it is not alone sufficient that [the Court]
would decide a case differently now than [it] did then.”

39

Kimble, 576 U.S. at 455. “Indeed, stare decisis has consequence only to the extent it sustains incorrect decisions.” Ibid. And even a “good argument” that the Court
“got [it] wrong” “cannot by itself justify scrapping settled
precedent.” Ibid. Instead, the Court “consider[s] the
egregiousness of the precedent’s error.” NRSC, 146
S. Ct. at 2424.
a. Whatever might be said of Bivens, Carlson was
not egregiously wrong. Even after the Court eliminated
general federal common law in Erie R.R. Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64, 78 (1938), it retains common-lawmaking authority in certain limited “enclaves” where
uniquely federal interests are at stake, Banco Nacional
de Cuba v. Sabbatino, 376 U.S. 398, 426 (1964); see also
Boyle v. United Techs. Corp., 487 U.S. 500, 504 (1988)
(noting that federal courts may still formulate federal
common law in certain areas implicating “uniquely federal interests” (citation omitted)). One such enclave involves “the civil liability of federal officials for actions
taken in the course of their duty.” Boyle, 487 U.S. at 505
& n.1 (“[T]he liability of federal officials … is an area of
uniquely federal interest.”).
Carlson claims at least arguably fall within a federal
enclave. In addition to affecting “the civil liability of federal officials for actions taken in the course of their
duty,” id. at 505, Carlson claims concern the conduct of
federal officers in a physical federal enclave. The plaintiff is in prison only because of a federal conviction before a federal court for violating a federal statute. These
circumstances give rise to corollary duties: Because of
the nature of prisons, “[a]n inmate must rely on prison
authorities to treat his medical needs,” and thus “‘[i]t is
but just that the public be required to care for the pris-

40

oner, who cannot by reason of the deprivation of his liberty, care for himself.’” Estelle v. Gamble, 429 U.S. 97,
103-04 (1976) (citation omitted).
This application of federal common law to apportion
liability is not novel. In Boyle, the Court invoked federal
common law to justify immunity for government contractors from liability for design defects. 487 U.S. at 504-
06. In Harlow v. Fitzgerald, the Court again relied on
federal common law to define the qualified -immunity
standard for federal officers. 457 U.S. 800, 806 , 818
(1982). And even McCarthy arguably rested on federal
common law regarding prudential exhaustion of administrative remedies for a Carlson claim. See 503 U.S. at
152-56. These uses of federal common law are no less
significant than Carlson in terms of allocating liability
between aggrieved individuals and federal officers.
Carlson follows a long tradition of damages claims
against prison officers who violate their duties to prisoners. Anglo-American law regularly tested the legality
of official conduct through damages actions against the
responsible officer. See Tanzin v. Tanvir, 592 U.S. 43,
49 (2020); Little v. Barreme, 6 U.S. ( 2 Cranch) 170
(1804); Elliott v. Swartwout, 35 U.S. ( 10 Pet. ) 137
(1836); Mitchell v. Harmony, 54 U.S. (13 How.) 115, 137
(1851); Buck v. Colbath, 70 U.S. ( 3 Wall. ) 334, 344
(1865); Belknap v. Schild, 161 U.S. 10, 18 (1896). Such
cases predate the Founding. See, e.g., Huckle v. Money,
(1763) 95 Eng. Rep. 768 (C.P.) (action for false imprisonment).
The historical foundation for Carlson claims is especially strong, because the common law imposed on the
jailer a duty to provide (or allow others to provide) a
prisoner with the necessities of life. At common law, an
imprisoned debtor could maintain a civil action against

41

a gaoler, who , acting out of “ [m]alice … keep[s] his
[v]ictuals from him, by reason whereof he is so spent,
that he becomes lame, or hath other [i]nfirmity.” 1 Anthony Fitz-Herbert, The New Natura Brevium 212 (8th
ed. 1755). Courts also recognized the availability of a
civil action by a prisoner against the sheriff as supervisor of an officer who left the prisoner exposed to the cold.
See, e.g., Rex v. Huggins (1730) 92 Eng. Rep. 518, 522
(K.B.) (“It has been settled, that … a sheriff must answer for the offences of his gaoler civilly.”); cf. William
Style, Narrationes Modernae 432 (London, 1658) (dismissing habeas claim for “us[ing] [the prisoner] hardly,”
but observing that the prisoner could “bring an [a]ction
against him” at law).
After the Founding, courts in the United States adhered to that tradition, recognizing that “[i]t is the duty
of all keepers of jails and prisons to treat their prisoners
humanely.” City of Topeka v. Boutwell, 35 P. 819, 822
(Kan. 1894). “For all needless sufferings and indignities
which they impose they are accountable in damages to
the party injured.” Ibid.; see also Tennessee ex rel. Morris v. Nat’l Sur. Co., 39 S.W.2d 581, 583 (Tenn. 1931)
(overruling demurrer to claim alleging the failure of the
sheriff and deputy, “knowing [the prisoner’s] urgent
need of medical and surgical attention” to obtain
“prompt and proper medical and surgical attention and
services” (quotation marks omitted)).
Carlson is therefore best understood as an application of the Court’s federal common-law power to recognize that the common law “apparently authorized prisoner lawsuits to recover damages” in this narrow context. Richardson v. McKnight, 521 U.S. 399, 407 (1997)
(citing 2 C. Addison, A Treatise on the Law of Torts
§ 1016, pp. 224-25 (1876)). Unlike Bivens claims—which

42

arise inside the home—Carlson claims concern the conduct of federal officers in a federal prison overseeing federal prisoners incarcerated pursuant to a federal conviction. The liability Carlson imposes flows from a long tradition of common-law causes of action in the prison context specifically. There is nothing “egregiously wrong”
about using the Court’s common-law authority to continue that tradition in this context.
b. Nielsen argues that Bivens (and by extension
Carlson) cannot be justified as “the work of a commonlaw court” because of “the demise of federal general common law.” Pet. Br. 44 (quoting Hernandez, 589 U.S. at
100-01). But that ignores that at least for Carlson, there
is substantial basis in the law for the creation of common law in such a discrete federal enclave. The United
States likewise urges that this analysis would justify all
Bivens claims (which are necessarily brought against
federal officers), U.S. Br. 29-30, but that overlooks the
additional, unique federal dimensions of a Carlson
claim, such as the existence of a federal conviction and
a federally administered institution. Bivens claims, by
contrast, arise in the home  and concern the rights of
wholly private individuals not subject to constant federal supervision or dependent on federal officials for the
necessities of life.
Whether the Court today agrees with the use of federal common law to justify the creation of a Carlson action, see Pet. Br. 42-44, it was at least not “egregiously
wrong” for Carlson to exercise that power in this narrow
context. NRSC, 146 S.  Ct. at 2424. Unlike other decisions this Court has recently repudiated, Carlson is not
divorced from “text, history, or precedent.” Dobbs v.
Jackson Women’s Health Org., 597 U.S. 215, 270 (2022).
Nor has Carlson “been difficult to make sense of from

43

the start,” creating artificial categories by “‘blind feats
of definition.’” Trump v. Slaughter, 146 S.  Ct. 2283,
2302 (2026) (citation omitted). Even if wrong under today’s jurisprudence, Carlson finds ample footing in the
law.3
2. Reliance on Carlson is concrete and unusually
weighty
The second stare decisis factor—reliance—is powerful here. As set forth above, the Westfall Act and the
PLRA are best understood as ratifying Carlson, foreclosing Nielsen’s and the government’s arguments for overruling Carlson. But at the very least, those statutes
show that Congress has relied on Carlson and its progeny, weighing heavily against overruling Carlson.
The reliance inquiry “focuses on the legitimate expectations of those who have reasonably relied on the precedent” and may account for “the age of the precedent.”
Ramos v. Louisiana, 590 U.S. 83 , 122 (2020) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring in part). And reliance interests
carry significant weight when they emanate from the
legislature. See Hilton v. S.C. Pub. Rys. Comm’n, 502
U.S. 197, 202 (1991).
In Hilton, the Court declined to overrule its previous
decision permitting damages actions against state agencies under the Federal Employers’ Liability Act (FELA).
502 U.S. at 201-02. The Court’s decision rested largely
on States’ legislative reliance. Ibid. The Court observed

3  Nielsen urges that Bivens was premised on the view that “courts
should create damages remedies to effectuate the perceived purposes of statutes lacking such remedies,” Pet. Br. 42, but he overlooks that this Court had repudiated that view by the time Carlson
was decided in 1980 , see Transamerica Mortg. Advisors Inc. v.
Lewis, 444 U.S. 11 (1979).

44

that many States had passed laws exempting certain
employees from workers’ compensation laws on the belief that those employees could file FELA suits against
their state employers. Id. at 202 -03. The Court explained that “[s]tare decisis has added force when the
legislature, in the public sphere, … ha[s] acted in reliance on a previous decision,” and that the Court should
avoid a decision that “would … require an extensive legislative response.” Id. at 202.
The circumstances here are remarkably similar to
Hilton. When Congress passed the Westfall Act and
eliminated state-law remedies for a constitutional violation, it did so on the understanding that Bivens and
Carlson claims could continue to be brought. See H.R.
Rep. No. 100-700, at 6 (1988). As in Hilton, the legislature relied on this Court’s recognition of a private right
of action to take away a preexisting right of action that
provided the same remedy. Indeed, the legislative history confirms Congress’s reliance, expressing the view
that Bivens and Carlson cases concern “a more serious
intrusion of the rights of an individual that merits special attention.” Ibid. To eliminate Carlson claims now,
decades after Congress passed the Westfall Act, would
upend that reliance.
Nielsen asserts that if Congress has in fact relied on
Bivens or Carlson, “‘that is precisely the problem,’” because Congress has “less incentive to legislate (or an excuse not to).” Pet. Br. 47 (quoting Slaughter, 146 S. Ct.
at 2303). But Congress has legislated, undertaking precisely the kind of “weigh[ing] [of] policy considerations”
the Court has long said is Congress’s duty. Egbert, 596
U.S. at 491. And unlike in Slaughter—where Congress
had relied on the existing precedent only to arrogate
power properly belonging to the Executive, see 146

45

S. Ct. at 2310—here, Congress had every incentive to
expressly eliminate Carlson claims altogether if it had
intended to do so. Instead, it preserved those claims and
devised nuanced requirements for bringing them. That
is legislative reliance, just like in Hilton.
3. The jurisprudential and real -world effects of
Carlson favor its preservation
The final stare decisis factor—the practical and realworld consequences of overturning Carlson—also
weighs in favor of retaining Carlson.
The practical effect of overruling Carlson would be
stark. As this Court has recognized, prisoners are
wholly dependent on prison officials for access to medical care. See Estelle, 429 U.S. at 103 -04. Overruling
Carlson would leave federal prisoners without a damages remedy against the responsible officer for completed constitutional injuries. Federal prisoners could
be subject to cruel and prolonged agony with no remedy
at all . Even Nielsen acknowledges —and history
shows—that such remedies have long existed and have
never before been foreclosed entirely. T he judiciary
would thus fail to act as an “impenetrable bulwark …
naturally led to resist every encroachment upon [constitutionally enumerated] rights.” 1 Annals of Cong. 439
(1789) (statement of Rep. James Madison).
Overruling Carlson would also have the anomalous
effect of making injunctive relief the primary mechanism for enforcement of constitutional rights in prison,
as Nielsen repeatedly urges. See Pet. Br. 18, 25-26, 34,
38. That is the inverse of the longstanding rule that injunctive relief is available only if “remedies available at
law, such as monetary damages, are inadequate.” eBay,
547 U.S. at 391; Watson v. Sutherland, 72 U.S. (5 Wall.)

46

74, 79 (1866) (“The absence of a plain and adequate remedy at law affords the only test of equity jurisdiction.”).
Several provisions of the PLRA are intended specifically
to limit the injunctive relief available to prisoners, see
18 U.S.C. 3626(a)(1)(A)-(C), (a)(2) and (b)(1)-(3), reaffirming Congress’s judgment that damages are the ordinary remedy. Eliminating a damages remedy to make
way for injunctive relief flips equity on its head.
Nielsen contends that Bivens—and presumably
Carlson—is unworkable, citing lower -court disagreements that have arisen since Egbert. Pet. Br. 45. But
this Court’s decision in this case will resolve those disagreements. And applying Carlson’s settled context is
straightforward: It provides a federal prisoner with an
individual-capacity Eighth Amendment action against
federal prison personnel responsible for deliberate indifference to an objectively serious medical need. See 446
U.S. at 16-17 & n.1. The standard for such claims was
articulated in Estelle, 429 U.S. 97, and lower courts in
both the Carlson context and the Section 1983 context
have developed a robust body of law for assessing such
claims. Qualified immunity and the PLRA protect officers from frivolous or burdensome litigation that could
interfere with their duties. See Carlson, 446 U.S. at 19.
Finally, Nielsen argues that determining whether
Carlson applies in a particular case requires the exercise of legislative judgment. Pet. Br. 31. It is not a legislative task to determine whe ther a case presents a
“meaningful” difference from a prior one. Abbasi, 582
U.S. at 139-40. That is an ordinary judicial exercise. Applying Carlson in its existing context does not require
anything other than the application of precedent called
for in every case.

This Court can and should resolve this case by following the path articulated in Cisco Systems: “[T]his far
and no further.” 146 S. Ct. at 1 892 n.3. Watanabe’s
claim falls in the heartland of Carlson. And the very separation of powers principles that Nielsen and the United
States invoke favor deference to Congress’s legislation
relying on and ratifying Carlson. The Court should affirm.

For the foregoing reasons, the judgment of the court
of appeals should be affirmed.

any hearing held at the facility.
(g) WAIVER OF REPLY
(1) Any defendant may waive the right to reply to
any action brought by a prisoner confined in any jail,
prison, or other correctional facility under section
1983 of this title or any other Federal law.

6a
Notwithstanding any other law or rule of procedure,
such waiver shall not constitute an admission of the
allegations contained in the complaint. No relief
shall be granted to the plaintiff unless a reply has
been filed.
(2) The court may require any defendant to reply to
a complaint brought under this section if it finds
that the plaintiff has a reasonable opportunity to
prevail on the merits.
(h) “PRISONER” DEFINED
As used in this section, the term “prisoner” means any
person incarcerated or detained in any facility who is
accused of, convicted of, sentenced for, or adjudicated
delinquent for, violations of criminal law or the terms
and conditions of parole, probation, pretrial release, or
diversionary program.

SUBJECT: ADMINISTRATIVE REMEDY OF
